Proposition 1.1
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.1}
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: Let $x,y\in X$ and suppose $d(x,y)=0$. By the triangle inequality,
\[
\label{eq:1.u5}
d(x,x)\le d(x,y)+d(y,x)=0+0=0,
\]
so $d(x,x)=0$. Again by the triangle inequality,
\[
\label{eq:1.u6}
d(x,y)\le d(x,x)+d(x,y)=0+d(x,y)=d(x,y),
\]
and similarly $d(y,y)=0$. Using the triangle inequality in the form $d(x,y)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y)$ with $z=x$ gives $d(x,y)\le d(x,x)+d(x,y)$, hence equality. By the metric axiom of definiteness, $d(x,y)=0$ implies $x=y$, so (2) holds.

$(2)\Rightarrow(3)$: Fix $x,y\in X$. If $x=y$, then $d(x,y)=d(x,x)=0$ by the metric axiom $d(x,x)=0$. Conversely, if $d(x,y)=0$, then $x=y$ by (2). Thus $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$.

$(3)\Rightarrow(1)$: For any $x\in X$, $x=x$, so by (3) one has $d(x,x)=0$.

Therefore (1), (2), and (3) are equivalent.
\end{proof}

Proposition 1.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.2}
Set $a_i=|x_i-y_i|\ge 0$ for $i=1,\dots,n$.

For the first inequality, since $a_i^2\le a_i\sum_{j=1}^n a_j$ for each $i$, summing over $i$ gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u12}
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2.
\]
Taking square roots yields $d_{\ell^2}(x,y)\le d_{\ell^1}(x,y)$.

For the second inequality, expand and use $2a_i a_j\le a_i^2+a_j^2$ for $i\ne j$:
\[
\label{eq:1.u13}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le n} a_i a_j
\le \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(a_i^2+a_j^2)
= n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2.
\]
Taking square roots yields $d_{\ell^1}(x,y)\le \sqrt{n}\, d_{\ell^2}(x,y)$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 1.8
Proposition 1.3
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.3}
Fix $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and set $v=x-y=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$. By definition, $d_{\ell^2}(x,y)=\|v\|_2$ and $d_{\ell^\infty}(x,y)=\|v\|_\infty$.

For the upper bound, since $\|v\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le n}|v_i|$, one has $|v_i|\le \|v\|_\infty$ for each $i$, hence
\[
\label{eq:1.u17}
\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n |v_i|^2 \ge \max_{1\le i\le n}|v_i|^2=\|v\|_\infty^2,
\]
so $\|v\|_\infty\le \|v\|_2$.

For the lower bound, again $|v_i|\le \|v\|_\infty$ for each $i$, so
\[
\label{eq:1.u18}
\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n |v_i|^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n \|v\|_\infty^2 = n\,\|v\|_\infty^2.
\]
Taking square roots yields $\|v\|_2\le \sqrt{n}\,\|v\|_\infty$, equivalently $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\,\|v\|_2\le \|v\|_\infty$.

Substituting $v=x-y$ gives the stated inequalities for $d_{\ell^2}$ and $d_{\ell^\infty}$.
\end{proof}

proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.5}
For $u,v\in\mathbf{R}^n$ set $a_j=|u_j-v_j|\ge 0$.

First note the pointwise inequalities
\[
\label{eq:1.u21}
d_{\ell^\infty}(u,v)=\max_j a_j\le \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j^2\Bigr)^{1/2}=d_{\ell^2}(u,v)\le \sum_{j=1}^n a_j=d_{\ell^1}(u,v).
\]
Also, since $a_j\le \max_i a_i$ for each $j$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u22}
d_{\ell^1}(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\le n\max_j a_j= n\,d_{\ell^\infty}(u,v),
\]
and therefore
\[
\label{eq:1.u23}
d_{\ell^2}(u,v)=\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n (\max_i a_i)^2\Bigr)^{1/2}=\sqrt{n}\,d_{\ell^\infty}(u,v).
\]

(a)$\Rightarrow$(c): If $d_{\ell^2}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$, then by $d_{\ell^\infty}\le d_{\ell^2}$, also $d_{\ell^\infty}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$.

(c)$\Rightarrow$(b): If $d_{\ell^\infty}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$, then $d_{\ell^1}(x^{(k)},x)\le n\,d_{\ell^\infty}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$.

(b)$\Rightarrow$(a): If $d_{\ell^1}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$, then by $d_{\ell^2}\le d_{\ell^1}$, also $d_{\ell^2}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0$.

(c)$\Leftrightarrow$(d):
Assume (c). For each fixed $j$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u24}
|x_j^{(k)}-x_j|\le \max_{1\le i\le n}|x_i^{(k)}-x_i|=d_{\ell^\infty}(x^{(k)},x)\to 0,
\]
so $x_j^{(k)}\to x_j$ in $\mathbf{R}$.
Conversely, assume (d). Given $\varepsilon>0$, for each $j$ there exists $K_j$ such that $|x_j^{(k)}-x_j|<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K_j$. Let $K=\max_{1\le j\le n} K_j$. Then for all $k\ge K$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u25}
d_{\ell^\infty}(x^{(k)},x)=\max_{1\le j\le n}|x_j^{(k)}-x_j|<\varepsilon,
\]
so (c) holds.

The implications above show (a), (b), (c), (d) are equivalent.
\end{proof}

Proposition 1.8
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.8}
The map $d'$ takes values in $[0,\infty)$ since $d$ does.

For $x,y\in X$, symmetry follows from symmetry of $d$:
\[
\label{eq:1.u30}
d'(x,y)=d(f(x),f(y))=d(f(y),f(x))=d'(y,x).
\]

For $x,y\in X$, $d'(x,y)=0$ if and only if $d(f(x),f(y))=0$, which holds if and only if $f(x)=f(y)$ since $d$ is a metric. Since $f$ is injective, $f(x)=f(y)$ implies $x=y$. Conversely, if $x=y$ then $d'(x,y)=d(f(x),f(x))=0$. Hence $d'(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$.

For the triangle inequality, let $x,y,z\in X$. Then
\[
\label{eq:1.u31}
d'(x,z)=d(f(x),f(z))\le d(f(x),f(y))+d(f(y),f(z))=d'(x,y)+d'(y,z),
\]
using the triangle inequality for $d$.

Thus $d'$ satisfies nonnegativity, symmetry, identity of indiscernibles, and the triangle inequality, so $d'$ is a metric on $X$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 1.9
Theorem 1.1
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.1}
If $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2=0$, then $b_i=0$ for all $i$, hence $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i=0$ and the inequality holds. Assume $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2>0$.

For $t\in\mathbb{R}$ define
\[
\label{eq:1.u37}
P(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-t b_i)^2.
\]
Then $P(t)\ge 0$ for all $t$. Expanding,
\[
\label{eq:1.u38}
P(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2-2t\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i+t^2\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2.
\]
This is a quadratic polynomial in $t$ with leading coefficient $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2>0$ that is nonnegative for all $t$, so its discriminant is nonpositive:
\[
\label{eq:1.u39}
\bigl(-2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\bigr)^2-4\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\Bigr)\le 0.
\]
Hence
\[
\label{eq:1.u40}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2\le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right).
\]
Taking square roots gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u41}
\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right| \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 1.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.2}
If $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=0$ or $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2=0$, then $a_i=0$ for all $i$ or $b_i=0$ for all $i$, and the inequality is immediate. Assume henceforth that
\[
\label{eq:1.u43}
A:=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2>0,\qquad B:=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2>0.
\]
For $t\in\mathbb{R}$ define
\[
\label{eq:1.u44}
f(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i t-b_i)^2= A t^2-2\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)t + B.
\]
Since $f(t)$ is a sum of squares, $f(t)\ge 0$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. The discriminant of this quadratic therefore satisfies
\[
\label{eq:1.u45}
\Delta = \left(-2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2-4AB \le 0,
\]
which yields the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
\[
\label{eq:1.u46}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2\le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)=AB.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\label{eq:1.u47}
\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i+b_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i + \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2
\le A + 2\sqrt{AB} + B = (\sqrt{A}+\sqrt{B})^2.
\]
Taking square roots (both sides are nonnegative) gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u48}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i+b_i)^2\right)^{1/2} \le \sqrt{A}+\sqrt{B}
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)^{1/2}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 1.10
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.10}
By the triangle inequality,
\[
\label{eq:1.u50}
d(x,y)\le d(x,x_n)+d(x_n,y_n)+d(y_n,y)
\]
so
\[
\label{eq:1.u51}
d(x,y)-d(x_n,y_n)\le d(x,x_n)+d(y_n,y).
\]
Similarly,
\[
\label{eq:1.u52}
d(x_n,y_n)\le d(x_n,x)+d(x,y)+d(y,y_n)
\]
so
\[
\label{eq:1.u53}
d(x_n,y_n)-d(x,y)\le d(x_n,x)+d(y,y_n).
\]
Combining these inequalities yields
\[
\label{eq:1.u54}
\bigl|d(x_n,y_n)-d(x,y)\bigr|\le d(x_n,x)+d(y_n,y).
\]
Since $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$, the right-hand side tends to $0$, hence $d(x_n,y_n)\to d(x,y)$.
\end{proof}

proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.3}
First, $\operatorname{int}(E)\cap\operatorname{ext}(E)=\varnothing$ since $\operatorname{int}(E)\subseteq E$ and $\operatorname{ext}(E)=\operatorname{int}(X\setminus E)\subseteq X\setminus E$.

To show $\overline{E}=X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)$, let $x\in X$.

If $x\in\operatorname{ext}(E)$, then there exists $r>0$ such that $B(x,r)\subseteq X\setminus E$, hence $B(x,r)\cap E=\varnothing$, so $x\notin\overline{E}$. Therefore $\overline{E}\subseteq X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)$.

Conversely, if $x\notin\overline{E}$, then by definition there exists $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\cap E=\varnothing$, i.e. $B(x,r)\subseteq X\setminus E$, so $x\in\operatorname{int}(X\setminus E)=\operatorname{ext}(E)$. Thus $X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)\subseteq\overline{E}$, and hence $\overline{E}=X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)$.

By the definition of boundary, $\partial E = X\setminus(\operatorname{int}(E)\cup\operatorname{ext}(E))$, so
\[
\label{eq:1.u65}
\operatorname{int}(E)\cup\partial E
= \operatorname{int}(E)\cup\bigl(X\setminus(\operatorname{int}(E)\cup\operatorname{ext}(E))\bigr)
= X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E),
\]
using $\operatorname{int}(E)\cap\operatorname{ext}(E)=\varnothing$.
Combining with $\overline{E}=X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)$ gives $\overline{E}=\operatorname{int}(E)\cup\partial E=X\setminus\operatorname{ext}(E)$.
\end{proof}

Proposition 1.18
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.18}
(a) Assume that $E$ is open in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$. For each $x\in E$ there exists $r_x>0$ such that
\[
\label{eq:1.u68}
B_Y(x,r_x):=\{y\in Y: d(x,y)<r_x\}\subseteq E.
\]
Define
\[
\label{eq:1.u69}
V:=\bigcup_{x\in E} B_X(x,r_x),\qquad B_X(x,r_x):=\{z\in X: d(x,z)<r_x\}.
\]
Then $V$ is open in $X$. Moreover, $E\subseteq V\cap Y$ since each $x\in E$ lies in $B_X(x,r_x)$. Conversely, if $y\in V\cap Y$, then $y\in B_X(x,r_x)$ for some $x\in E$, hence $d(x,y)<r_x$ and $y\in Y$, so $y\in B_Y(x,r_x)\subseteq E$. Thus $V\cap Y\subseteq E$, and therefore $E=V\cap Y$.

Conversely, assume $E=V\cap Y$ for some open $V\subseteq X$. Let $x\in E$. Since $x\in V$ and $V$ is open, there exists $r>0$ such that $B_X(x,r)\subseteq V$. Then
\[
\label{eq:1.u70}
B_Y(x,r)=B_X(x,r)\cap Y\subseteq V\cap Y=E,
\]
so $x$ is an interior point of $E$ in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$. Hence $E$ is open in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$.

(b) If $E$ is closed in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$, then $Y\setminus E$ is open in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$. By part (a) there exists an open set $V\subseteq X$ such that $Y\setminus E=V\cap Y$. Let $K:=X\setminus V$, which is closed in $X$. Then
\[
\label{eq:1.u71}
E=Y\setminus (V\cap Y)=Y\cap (X\setminus V)=Y\cap K.
\]
Conversely, if $E=K\cap Y$ for some closed $K\subseteq X$, then $X\setminus K$ is open in $X$ and
\[
\label{eq:1.u72}
Y\setminus E=Y\setminus (K\cap Y)=Y\cap (X\setminus K).
\]
By part (a), $Y\setminus E$ is open in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$, so $E$ is closed in $(Y,d|_{Y\times Y})$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 1.23

proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.23}
Reflexivity: If $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, then $d(x_n,x_n)=0$ for all $n$, hence $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,x_n)=0$, so $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n$.

Symmetry: If $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} y_n$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,y_n)=0$. Since $d(x_n,y_n)=d(y_n,x_n)$ for all $n$, it follows that $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(y_n,x_n)=0$, hence $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} y_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n$.

Transitivity: Suppose $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} y_n$ and $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} y_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} z_n$. Then
\[
\label{eq:1.u88}
\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,y_n)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \lim_{n\to\infty} d(y_n,z_n)=0.
\]
By the triangle inequality,
\[
\label{eq:1.u89}
d(x_n,z_n) \le d(x_n,y_n)+d(y_n,z_n)\quad\text{for all }n.
\]
Taking limits and using that the limit of a sum is the sum of limits gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u90}
\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,z_n) \le \lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,y_n)+\lim_{n\to\infty} d(y_n,z_n)=0,
\]
so $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,z_n)=0$. Hence $\mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} x_n \sim \mathrm{LIM}_{n\to\infty} z_n$.

Therefore $\sim$ is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 1.24

proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:1.24}
First, the limit in the definition of $d_{\overline X}$ exists for any Cauchy sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$. Indeed, for $m,n\in\mathbb N$ the triangle inequality gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u92}
\bigl|d(x_n,y_n)-d(x_m,y_m)\bigr|\le d(x_n,x_m)+d(y_n,y_m).
\]
Since $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy, the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $m,n\to\infty$, so $(d(x_n,y_n))$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb R$ and therefore convergent.

Well-definedness: suppose $(x_n)\sim (x_n')$ and $(y_n)\sim (y_n')$, i.e. $d(x_n,x_n')\to 0$ and $d(y_n,y_n')\to 0$. For each $n$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u93}
\bigl|d(x_n,y_n)-d(x_n',y_n')\bigr|\le d(x_n,x_n')+d(y_n,y_n')
\]
by two applications of the triangle inequality. Taking $n\to\infty$ yields
\[
\label{eq:1.u94}
\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,y_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n',y_n'),
\]
so $d_{\overline X}$ depends only on the equivalence classes.

Metric axioms: for $[(x_n)],[(y_n)],[(z_n)]\in\overline X$,
\begin{itemize}
\item Nonnegativity is immediate since $d(x_n,y_n)\ge 0$ for all $n$, hence $d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(y_n)])\ge 0$.
\item Symmetry holds since $d(x_n,y_n)=d(y_n,x_n)$ for all $n$, hence $d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(y_n)])=d_{\overline X}([(y_n)],[(x_n)])$.
\item Triangle inequality: for all $n$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u95}
d(x_n,z_n)\le d(x_n,y_n)+d(y_n,z_n).
\]
Taking limits gives
\[
\label{eq:1.u96}
d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(z_n)])\le d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(y_n)])+d_{\overline X}([(y_n)],[(z_n)]).
\]
\item Identity of indiscernibles: if $d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(y_n)])=0$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x_n,y_n)=0$, so $(x_n)\sim (y_n)$ and thus $[(x_n)]=[(y_n)]$. Conversely, if $[(x_n)]=[(y_n)]$, then $d(x_n,y_n)\to 0$, hence $d_{\overline X}([(x_n)],[(y_n)])=0$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore $d_{\overline X}$ is a metric on $\overline X$.
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 1.4

proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.4}
Let $\bigl(\xi^k\bigr)_{k\ge 1}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\overline X,d_{\overline X})$. Choose for each $k$ a representative Cauchy sequence $x^k=(x^k_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $X$ such that $\xi^k=[(x^k_n)]$.

Since $(\xi^k)$ is Cauchy, for each $m\ge 1$ there exists an index $K_m$ such that
\[
\label{eq:1.u98}
d_{\overline X}(\xi^k,\xi^\ell)<2^{-m}\quad\text{for all }k,\ell\ge K_m.
\]
Fix $m$ and apply this with $k=K_m$ and $\ell=K_{m+1}$ to obtain
\[
\label{eq:1.u99}
d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi^{K_{m+1}})<2^{-m}.
\]
By the definition of $d_{\overline X}$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u100}
\lim_{n\to\infty} d\bigl(x^{K_m}_n, x^{K_{m+1}}_n\bigr) = d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi^{K_{m+1}}) < 2^{-m}.
\]
Hence there exists an integer $N_m$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diag}
 d\bigl(x^{K_m}_{N_m}, x^{K_{m+1}}_{N_m}\bigr) < 2^{-m}\quad\text{for all }m\ge 1.
\end{equation}
Define a sequence $(z_m)_{m\ge 1}$ in $X$ by
\[
\label{eq:1.u101}
z_m := x^{K_m}_{N_m}.
\]

Claim 1: $(z_m)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$. Let $p>m$. By the triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:diag},
\[
\label{eq:1.u102}
d(z_m,z_p) \le \sum_{j=m}^{p-1} d(z_j,z_{j+1}) = \sum_{j=m}^{p-1} d\bigl(x^{K_j}_{N_j},x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_{j+1}}\bigr).
\]
Insert and subtract $x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_j}$ to get
\[
\label{eq:1.u103}
d\bigl(x^{K_j}_{N_j},x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_{j+1}}\bigr) \le d\bigl(x^{K_j}_{N_j},x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_j}\bigr) + d\bigl(x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_j},x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_{j+1}}\bigr).
\]
The first term is $<2^{-j}$ by \eqref{eq:diag}. Since each $x^{K_{j+1}}$ is Cauchy, $N_{j+1}$ can be chosen (in addition to \eqref{eq:diag}) so that
\[
\label{eq:1.u104}
d\bigl(x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_j},x^{K_{j+1}}_{N_{j+1}}\bigr)<2^{-j}.
\]
Thus $d(z_j,z_{j+1})<2^{-(j-1)}$ for all $j$, and therefore
\[
\label{eq:1.u105}
d(z_m,z_p) \le \sum_{j=m}^{\infty} 2^{-(j-1)} = 2^{-(m-2)},
\]
which tends to $0$ as $m\to\infty$. Hence $(z_m)$ is Cauchy.

Let $\xi := [(z_m)]\in\overline X$.

Claim 2: $\xi^k\to \xi$ in $(\overline X,d_{\overline X})$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $m$ such that $2^{-(m-2)}<\varepsilon/2$. Since $(\xi^k)$ is Cauchy, for all $k\ge K_m$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u106}
d_{\overline X}(\xi^k,\xi^{K_m})<\varepsilon/2.
\]
It suffices to show $d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi)<\varepsilon/2$. By definition,
\[
\label{eq:1.u107}
d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi) = \lim_{r\to\infty} d\bigl(x^{K_m}_r, z_r\bigr).
\]
For $r\ge m$, write
\[
\label{eq:1.u108}
d\bigl(x^{K_m}_r, z_r\bigr) = d\bigl(x^{K_m}_r, x^{K_r}_{N_r}\bigr) \le d\bigl(x^{K_m}_r, x^{K_m}_{N_m}\bigr) + d\bigl(x^{K_m}_{N_m}, x^{K_r}_{N_r}\bigr).
\]
The first term tends to $0$ as $r\to\infty$ because $x^{K_m}$ is Cauchy and $N_m$ is fixed. For the second term, use the triangle inequality along the chain $z_m,z_{m+1},\dots,z_r$ to obtain
\[
\label{eq:1.u109}
d\bigl(x^{K_m}_{N_m}, x^{K_r}_{N_r}\bigr)=d(z_m,z_r)\le \sum_{j=m}^{r-1} d(z_j,z_{j+1}) \le \sum_{j=m}^{\infty} 2^{-(j-1)} = 2^{-(m-2)} < \varepsilon/2.
\]
Taking $r\to\infty$ yields $d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi)\le \varepsilon/2$. Therefore for all $k\ge K_m$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u110}
d_{\overline X}(\xi^k,\xi)\le d_{\overline X}(\xi^k,\xi^{K_m})+d_{\overline X}(\xi^{K_m},\xi) < \varepsilon.
\]
Hence $(\xi^k)$ converges to $\xi$ in $\overline X$, proving that $(\overline X,d_{\overline X})$ is complete.
\end{proof}

Theorem 1.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.6}
\emph{Closedness.} It suffices to show that $X\setminus Y$ is open. Let $x\in X\setminus Y$. For each $y\in Y$ define $r_y:=\tfrac12 d(x,y)>0$ and consider the open balls $B(y,r_y)$. The family $\{B(y,r_y): y\in Y\}$ is an open cover of $Y$. By compactness, there exist $y_1,\dots,y_n\in Y$ such that
\[
\label{eq:1.u119}
Y\subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n B(y_i,r_{y_i}).
\]
Set
\[
\label{eq:1.u120}
\delta:=\min_{1\le i\le n} r_{y_i} >0.
\]
The claim is that $B(x,\delta)\subseteq X\setminus Y$. Suppose $z\in B(x,\delta)$ and $z\in Y$. Then $z\in B(y_i,r_{y_i})$ for some $i$, hence
\[
\label{eq:1.u121}
d(x,y_i)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y_i) < \delta + r_{y_i} \le r_{y_i}+r_{y_i}=d(x,y_i),
\]
a contradiction. Therefore $B(x,\delta)\cap Y=\varnothing$, so $x$ is an interior point of $X\setminus Y$. Since $x\in X\setminus Y$ was arbitrary, $X\setminus Y$ is open and $Y$ is closed.

\emph{Boundedness.} Fix $x_0\in X$. The family of open balls $\{B(x_0,m): m\in \mathbb{N}\}$ covers $X$ and hence covers $Y$. By compactness, there exist $m_1,\dots,m_k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
\label{eq:1.u122}
Y\subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^k B(x_0,m_j).
\]
Let $R:=\max_{1\le j\le k} m_j$. Then $Y\subseteq B(x_0,R)$, so $Y$ is bounded.
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 1.7
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.7}
All three listed metrics induce the same topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$, hence compactness, closedness, and boundedness are the same for each of them. It therefore suffices to prove the statement for the Euclidean metric $\|\cdot\|$.

$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: Assume $E$ is compact.

First, $E$ is bounded. If $E$ were unbounded, then for each $m\in\mathbb{N}$ the set $U_m:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|<m\}$ is open and $\{U_m\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$ covers $E$. Any finite subcollection has the form $\{U_{m_1},\dots,U_{m_k}\}$, whose union equals $U_M$ with $M:=\max\{m_1,\dots,m_k\}$, and $U_M$ cannot contain the unbounded set $E$. This contradicts compactness, so $E$ is bounded.

Second, $E$ is closed. Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus E$. For each $y\in E$ define $r_y:=\tfrac12\|x-y\|>0$ and the open ball $B(y,r_y)$. Then $\{B(y,r_y):y\in E\}$ is an open cover of $E$, so there exist $y_1,\dots,y_k\in E$ such that $E\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^k B(y_i,r_{y_i})$. Set
\[
\label{eq:1.u123}
\delta:=\min_{1\le i\le k} r_{y_i}>0.
\]
If $z\in B(x,\delta)$ and $z\in E$, then $z\in B(y_i,r_{y_i})$ for some $i$, so by the triangle inequality,
\[
\label{eq:1.u124}
\|x-y_i\|\le \|x-z\|+\|z-y_i\|<\delta+r_{y_i}\le r_{y_i}+r_{y_i}=\|x-y_i\|,
\]
a contradiction. Hence $B(x,\delta)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus E$, so $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus E$ is open and $E$ is closed.

$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$: Assume $E$ is closed and bounded. Boundedness implies there exists $R>0$ such that $E\subseteq [-R,R]^n$. The set $[-R,R]^n$ is compact: for each $m\in\mathbb{N}$ partition $[-R,R]^n$ into finitely many closed cubes of side length $\tfrac{2R}{m}$; choosing one point from each cube yields a finite set $F_m\subseteq [-R,R]^n$ such that for every $x\in [-R,R]^n$ there exists $p\in F_m$ with $\|x-p\|\le \tfrac{\sqrt{n}\,2R}{m}$. Thus $[-R,R]^n$ is totally bounded. It is also complete as a closed subset of the complete metric space $\mathbb{R}^n$. In a metric space, completeness plus total boundedness implies sequential compactness: given any sequence, choose a subsequence lying in one ball of radius $1$, then a further subsequence lying in a ball of radius $1/2$, and so on; the resulting nested choice is Cauchy, hence convergent. Therefore $[-R,R]^n$ is sequentially compact, hence compact.

Since $E$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$, it is also closed in the subspace $[-R,R]^n$. A closed subset of a compact metric space is compact: if $\{U_\alpha\}$ is an open cover of $E$, then $\{U_\alpha\}\cup\{[-R,R]^n\setminus E\}$ is an open cover of $[-R,R]^n$ and admits a finite subcover; removing $[-R,R]^n\setminus E$ yields a finite subcover of $E$. Hence $E$ is compact.
\end{proof}

Theorem 1.8
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:1.8}
Assume, for contradiction, that for every finite subset $F\subseteq A$ there exists a point of $Y$ not contained in $\bigcup_{\alpha\in F}V_{\alpha}$.

For $y\in Y$ define
\[
\label{eq:1.u127}
r(y):=\sup\bigl\{r\in(0,\infty): \exists\alpha\in A\text{ with }B_{(X,d)}(y,r)\subseteq V_{\alpha}\bigr\}.
\]
Since $y\in V_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha$ and $V_{\alpha}$ is open, there exists $\rho>0$ with $B(y,\rho)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$; hence $r(y)\ge \rho>0$ for all $y\in Y$. Set
\[
\label{eq:1.u128}
r_0:=\inf\{r(y):y\in Y\}\in[0,\infty].
\]

\emph{Case 1: $r_0=0$.} For each $n\ge 1$ choose $y^{(n)}\in Y$ with $r(y^{(n)})<1/n$. By compactness of $Y$, there exists a subsequence $y^{(n_j)}\to y_0\in Y$. Choose $\alpha\in A$ with $y_0\in V_{\alpha}$. Since $V_{\alpha}$ is open, there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $B(y_0,\varepsilon)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$. For sufficiently large $j$, $d(y^{(n_j)},y_0)<\varepsilon/2$, and then for any $z\in B(y^{(n_j)},\varepsilon/2)$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u129}
d(z,y_0)\le d(z,y^{(n_j)})+d(y^{(n_j)},y_0)<\varepsilon/2+\varepsilon/2=\varepsilon,
\]
so $z\in B(y_0,\varepsilon)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$. Thus $B(y^{(n_j)},\varepsilon/2)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$, which implies $r(y^{(n_j)})\ge \varepsilon/2$ for all large $j$, contradicting $r(y^{(n_j)})<1/n_j\to 0$.

\emph{Case 2: $0<r_0<\infty$.} Then $r(y)\ge r_0$ for all $y\in Y$, so for each $y\in Y$ there exists $\alpha\in A$ with $B(y,r_0/2)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$. Construct a sequence $(y^{(n)})_{n\ge 1}\subseteq Y$ inductively as follows. Choose any $y^{(1)}\in Y$. Suppose $y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(n)}$ have been chosen. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, choose $\alpha_j\in A$ with $B(y^{(j)},r_0/2)\subseteq V_{\alpha_j}$. If $Y\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^n B(y^{(j)},r_0/2)$, then
\[
\label{eq:1.u130}
Y\subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^n V_{\alpha_j},
\]
which is a finite subcover, contradicting the assumption. Hence there exists
\[
\label{eq:1.u131}
y^{(n+1)}\in Y\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^n B(y^{(j)},r_0/2).
\]
By construction, for all $k>j$ one has $d(y^{(k)},y^{(j)})\ge r_0/2$. In particular, for any $k>j$,
\[
\label{eq:1.u132}
d(y^{(k)},y^{(j)})\ge r_0/2>0,
\]
so $(y^{(n)})$ has no Cauchy subsequence. This contradicts compactness of $Y$, since every sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent (hence Cauchy) subsequence.

\emph{Case 3: $r_0=\infty$.} Then for each $y\in Y$ there exists $\alpha\in A$ with $B(y,1)\subseteq V_{\alpha}$. Repeating the construction of Case 2 with radius $1$ yields a sequence $(y^{(n)})$ in $Y$ such that $d(y^{(k)},y^{(j)})\ge 1$ for $k>j$, so again no subsequence is Cauchy, contradicting compactness.

Each case yields a contradiction, so there must exist a finite subset $F\subseteq A$ such that $Y\subseteq\bigcup_{\alpha\in F}V_{\alpha}$.
\end{proof}
